newsitem.title: USA: Republicans say Gore may have broken law on funds.
newsitem.headline: Republicans say Gore may have broken law on funds.

text.p: Congressional Republican leaders said Tuesday that Vice President Al Gore may have violated the law by soliciting campaign contributions from the White House.

They also reiterated their call for appointment of an independent counsel to investigate campaign financing irregularities one day after Gore asserted in a White House news conference that he had not broken the law.

"The law is clear that you should not be raising money on federal property and federal buildings," Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott told reporters. "It's there and if that's what happened then that itself would be enough to indicate that a special counsel should be appointed."
Lott, House Speaker Newt Gingrich and other Republican leaders were responding to a reporter's question during a photo taking session of a joint Republican meeting.
Gingrich charged that the Clinton campaign had violated campaign reform laws "on a grand scale."

"This is not 'everybody does it.' This is the most systematic large-scale effort to get around the law that we've certainly seen since Watergate, and in its total effort I think is much bigger than Watergate was," Gingrich said.

Representative Christopher Cox of California, a member of the House Republican leadership team, cited a memo written by former White House counsel Abner Mikva that campaign solicitations not be made from the White House.
"So the notion that somehow the vice president might be able to break this law whereas everyone else was not to do so ... was very odd indeed," Cox said.

Lott, without being specific, said he was looking into possible action by the Senate on a special counsel to examine campaign financing irregularities. Special counsels are named by a three-judge panel acting on the request of the attorney general.
Asked about the issue during testimony at a House hearing Tuesday, Attorney General Janet Reno said she had not excluded appointment of an independent counsel.

Referring to the Justice Department's own current investigation, she added: "But until the evidence and law dictate the appointment of an independent counsel I am going to do everything I can to pursue the allegations as vigorously as possible consistent with the evidence and the law."

Meanwhile, Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson, chairman of a Senate committee that is to investigate campaign financing, is reducing his request for funding of the investigation to $5.7 million from $6.5 million, a committee source said.

The Senate must approve the money but so far Democrats have refused to go along with Thompson's request and insist on $1.8 million to start the investigation, along with conditions that the probe end this year and a date be set to consider campaign finance legislation.
A fight over the funding could be waged on the Senate floor sometime this week, although no date has been set, the committee source said.
The source said that the group wants the FBI to assign 10 or 12 agents to help in the probe, which is expected to centre on illegal or improper foreign donations to the Democratic National Committee.
Republican leader Lott said he wanted to settle the funding matter with Democrats "without a big partisan shootout."
"I think the American people have heard enough. They want us to get on with it. They want us to look into the illegal actions that have occurred, if any," he told reporters.
Lott said people wanted to know who was involved in making foreign contributions to the Democratic campaign and whether there was any involvement by China.
He also rejected Democratic demands that congressional contributions and abuses be looked into as well as those of the Clinton campaign.
"The scope should be limited to illegal activities in the presidential campaign last year of either party."
